Confusable pairs from the lane travel pages, each tied to one manual page; knowledge-graph hints (group, difficulty, confusable pair) sit only in the trailing Why it matters line of each block.

FACT_ID: sec03-R01 | anchor: A02
Alleys and narrow residential areas carry the lowest statutory limit of 15 mph, while ordinary residential districts carry 25 mph, so the narrowness of the street changes the limit. [A02]
Why it matters: group statutory speeds; confusable narrow residential versus residential district; difficulty hard.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-R02 | anchor: A02
A school speed zone shares the 20 mph statutory limit with business districts, not the 25 mph limit that applies in residential districts and parks. [A02]
Why it matters: group statutory speeds; confusable school zone versus residential district; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-R03 | anchor: A02
The 55 mph statutory limit covers roads that fit no other category, while interstate highways have limits that vary rather than one fixed statutory figure. [A02]
Why it matters: group statutory speeds; confusable catch-all limit versus interstate; difficulty medium.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec03-R04 | anchor: A03
A yellow variable advisory speed sign only recommends a speed, while a black-and-white variable speed limit sign sets an enforceable limit that police treat like any other. [A03]
Why it matters: group variable signs; confusable advisory versus limit; difficulty hard.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec03-R05 | anchor: A04
The posted limit caps your speed in all conditions, while the basic rule can require going slower than that cap; neither one ever allows exceeding the limit. [A04]
Why it matters: group basic rule; confusable speed limit versus basic rule; difficulty medium.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-R06 | anchor: A04
A slow driver keeps to the right lane or right edge, except when getting ready to make a left turn. [A04]
Why it matters: group slow drivers; confusable keep right versus left-turn preparation; difficulty easy.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec03-R07 | anchor: A05
A broken yellow center line lets both directions pass, while a double solid yellow line bars passing for both directions but still allows a left turn across it once clear. [A05]
Why it matters: group yellow lines; confusable broken yellow versus double solid yellow; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-R08 | anchor: A05
In a solid-plus-broken yellow pair, only the line nearest your lane counts: broken on your side means you may pass, solid on your side means you may not. [A05]
Why it matters: group yellow lines; confusable your side versus the other side; difficulty hard.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec03-R09 | anchor: A06
A two-way left-turn lane is meant for waiting to turn left, while a painted median with double yellow lines may only be crossed to turn and never used as a turn lane. [A06]
Why it matters: group center areas; confusable two-way left-turn lane versus painted median; difficulty hard.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-R10 | anchor: A06
Yellow markings separate traffic going opposite ways, while white markings separate lanes going the same way and mark the right edge. [A06]
Why it matters: group line colors; confusable yellow versus white; difficulty easy.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec03-R11 | anchor: A07
A wide solid white line may be crossed but crossing is discouraged, a broken or dotted white line may be crossed with caution, and a double solid white line may not be crossed to change lanes. [A07]
Why it matters: group white lines; confusable wide solid versus broken versus double solid; difficulty hard.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R12 | anchor: A07
A dotted white line ahead of an exit means your lane will leave the route, while a dotted white line at a freeway on-ramp means you must merge into freeway traffic. [A07]
Why it matters: group white lines; confusable exit-only lane versus entrance merge; difficulty medium.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec03-R13 | anchor: A08
A stop line marks where you must stop, while a yield line of triangles pointing at you marks where you must yield. [A08]
Why it matters: group crossing markings; confusable stop line versus yield line; difficulty easy.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R14 | anchor: A08
A solid red lane is closed to cars, while striped red lines mark the places where a car may enter the transit lane to turn, park or reach a driveway. [A08]
Why it matters: group transit markings; confusable solid red versus striped red; difficulty medium.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec03-R15 | anchor: A09
The general safe following distance is two to four seconds, but at speeds above 30 mph the guidance rises to four seconds or more. [A09]
Why it matters: group following distance; confusable general gap versus higher-speed gap; difficulty medium.
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec03-R16 | anchor: A10
When a driver behind you wants to pass, you add following distance by slowing so there is room in front of you for them to complete the pass. [A10]
Why it matters: group following distance; confusable gap ahead versus gap behind; difficulty easy.
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec03-R17 | anchor: A12
With a tailgater behind you, easing off gradually is the advice, while braking hard to scare them off is never acceptable because it risks a rear-end crash. [A12]
Why it matters: group space behind; confusable gradual slowing versus brake-checking; difficulty easy.
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec03-R18 | anchor: A12
Mirrors alone are not enough for backing; the manual calls for turning your head and body to look out the rear window and glancing to each side. [A12]
Why it matters: group backing; confusable mirror check versus head turn; difficulty easy.
Source: [A12 -> pdf-0037]
